title: The bodhisattva precepts
hook: in East Asia and Tibet many lay people take bodhisattva vows as well as the five precepts
tomorrow: Taking vows as a lay person

segments.voice: Yesterday, a month of moon days: the uposatha on the new, full and half moons, a day and a night lived like the awakened. Did you find the moon? Day one thousand four hundred six.

The five precepts are mostly about what you don't do. Don't kill, don't steal, don't lie. They draw a line around your own conduct, and that line matters. But in East Asia and in Tibet, monks and lay people alike can take a second set of vows on top of the five. These ask for something different. They ask what you will do for others, and what you will refuse to do to them even in your heart. A Zen student, a grandmother at a temple in Taiwan, a Tibetan family at a ceremony with their lama: each might hold these vows. Today, the bodhisattva precepts.
screen: `THE FIVE PRECEPTS DRAW A LINE.` → `A SECOND SET OF VOWS.` → `WHAT YOU WILL DO FOR OTHERS.`

segments.voice: A bodhisattva is a being set on awakening, not only for themselves but for everyone. The bodhisattva precepts are the rules of that kind of life. In China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam, a widely used set comes from a text called the Brahma's Net Sutra. It lays out ten major precepts and forty-eight minor ones. The first few sound familiar: no killing, no stealing, no sexual misconduct, no lying, no selling intoxicants. But listen to how they're stretched. Not only don't kill, the text says, but don't encourage killing, don't praise it, don't make the means for it, and keep a heart of compassion that wants to protect life. Then come precepts the five never mention. Don't spread the faults of fellow Buddhists. Don't praise yourself while putting others down. Don't be stingy when someone asks for help, even with a teaching. Don't hold on to anger when someone apologizes. That last one is worth stopping on. It isn't only don't hit back. It's don't refuse the apology. In Tibet, the bodhisattva vow comes through a different line of texts and teachers, with its own list, but the turn is the same: the vow faces outward. The five precepts protect others from you. The bodhisattva precepts ask you to stand up for them. Some ceremonies also include three short pure precepts: avoid harm, do good, and help all beings. So the precepts become vows for others. Not just a fence around your own life, but a promise about everyone else's.
screen: `A BEING SET ON AWAKENING FOR ALL.` · `THE BRAHMA'S NET SUTRA.` · `DON'T REFUSE AN APOLOGY.` · then, large: `THE VOW FACES OUTWARD.`

segments.voice: Here's one precept from the Brahma's Net Sutra, in plain words: don't hold on to anger when someone asks to be forgiven. Sit with it for a moment, if you'd like. Breathe in and out a few times. Then let one person come to mind, someone who has said sorry to you, or tried to, maybe clumsily. Notice what happens in your chest and shoulders when you think of them. No need to fix it. Just notice whether the apology has been received yet. Then let the breath carry on. The bell holds the time.
The bodhisattva precepts. Vows taken on top of the five, facing outward: not only don't harm, but protect, help and forgive. Today's word.
Your line: vows for others. Today, when you hear someone's fault being discussed, see if you can be the one who doesn't add to it. Day one thousand four hundred six.

howItsDone: In East Asian Buddhism, monks, nuns and lay people may receive the bodhisattva precepts of the Brahma's Net Sutra in a ceremony, and in Tibetan Buddhism the bodhisattva vow is given by a lama; both are taken in addition to the five precepts.

fork.setup: someone who hurt you comes back and apologizes. under the Brahma's Net Sutra, what's the precept?
options: you may accept, if you feel like it.
don't hold on to anger; receive the apology.
stay polite but keep your distance forever.
fork.reveal: the text counts refusing an apology and holding on to anger among the major precepts. the vow faces outward.

original.note: Sanskrit bodhisattva (Pali bodhisatta): a being set on awakening; in the Mahayana, one who seeks it for all beings.

trapdoor: what you thought: precepts are a list of things not to do.
what it means: the bodhisattva precepts add vows for others: protect, help, forgive.
what a scholar hears: the ten major and forty-eight minor precepts of the Brahma's Net Sutra in East Asia, and the separate Tibetan bodhisattva vow tradition.

notes: This is the Mahayana Brahmajala Sutra (Fanwang jing), not the Pali Brahmajala Sutta (DN 1); the English name 'Brahma's Net Sutra' is used to keep them apart. Confirm naming.

Major precepts paraphrased: the first (killing, encouraging, praising, means of killing, with compassion), selling intoxicants, speaking of others' faults, praising self and disparaging others, stinginess with wealth or Dharma, harboring anger and refusing apology. Confirm order and wording.
'Ten major and forty-eight minor' is the text's own count. 'Best-known set' in East Asia is a soft superlative; consider softening to 'a widely used set' if a Keeper prefers.
Three pure precepts described as included in 'many of these ceremonies' (e.g. Zen jukai, Tendai); confirm or soften.
Tibetan bodhisattva vow 'through a different line of texts' (Asanga / Chandragomin lineages); kept general. Confirm.
Index hook says 'many lay people'; script avoids the count and says lay people 'can' take them.
Editor: sixth major precept matched to the text (spreading the faults of fellow Buddhists, not 'to look good', which overlapped the seventh); 'many of these ceremonies' softened to 'some ceremonies'.
